# Receipts of thought

> A receipt of thought is a signed, tamper-evident account of how a piece of writing was made, as presented by its author: the composition timeline, the passages an author discloses as AI-written, the claims they sourced and an embedded content credential. Anyone can verify one in a browser at receiptsofthought.com, with no server involved. The format and its verifier are open source under Apache-2.0.

When text is cheap to generate, a clean final draft is no longer evidence that someone thought. What stays scarce is the record of the work itself. A receipt makes that record verifiable: tampering after signing is detectable, and the check runs entirely client-side, so the file never leaves your machine.

## What a valid receipt proves

- Nothing in the receipt was altered after it was signed: the title, the text's fingerprint, the composition timeline, the disclosed AI passages and the sourced claims.
- Whether the published text is the text that was signed, when you hand the verifier that text as well. A receipt carries a fingerprint rather than the writing, so checked on its own it leaves that question open, and the page says which of the two it did.
- The composition timeline is exactly the one that was signed: no checkpoint has been reordered, inserted or removed since.
- The embedded C2PA-aligned content credential carries its own valid signature and binds the same text and the same key as the receipt around it.

## What it does not prove

- Who holds the signing key. A key belongs to a machine and its owner, not to a verified identity.
- That the timeline reflects honest work. The signature binds the timeline that was presented at signing, so an author could compose elsewhere, or prune the record, and sign the tidy version.
- That undisclosed text is human-written. Disclosure is the author's choice; the receipt binds what was disclosed, not what was not.

## How this differs from version history

A common question is whether this is what Google Docs version history already does. Partly, and when the reader can already open your document, version history is often enough. Four things are different. A receipt can be checked by a stranger, with no account, no access to the author's document and no trust in the company that made it, because verification runs in the reader's own browser. A receipt travels with the writing, so it can accompany a published article, a newsletter, a client deliverable or a submission, which an edit history cannot. A receipt carries counts and fingerprints of each draft rather than the draft text, so it is evidence an author can share without exposing everything they wrote and deleted. And a receipt records what the author chose to declare as AI-written, with the model named and the sources they checked, which an edit history does not model at all.

Neither can prove a person wrote something. Anyone determined to fake a composition history can type one out. A receipt is the author's account of how a piece was made, in a form that makes later changes detectable, and the claim stops there.

## How to verify one

Open [receiptsofthought.com](https://receiptsofthought.com/) and drop the `.receipts.json` file on the page. The check runs in the browser with WebCrypto: the file is never uploaded, and the page makes no network request while verifying, which its content security policy enforces. A verifier can also be built from the specification alone, and this one can be self-hosted.

## The pieces

- The verifier: [receiptsofthought.com](https://receiptsofthought.com/) checks a `.receipts.json` bundle in the browser.
- The format and verifier source: the open Apache-2.0 trust core, including the receipts format specification, the Ed25519 signing scheme and the client-side verifier.
- Folio: the desktop writing app for macOS and Linux that produces receipts as you write. Folio itself is proprietary; the format and verifier it produces receipts for are not, which is why a receipt can be checked without it.

## Who makes it

Ad Astra Computing. The receipts format and verifier are open so anyone can read, reimplement or host the verification.
